easy.heading: Warming Up With A Quick One
easy.body:
I hope your morning is going well! I just finished the easy Pips puzzle, and it was the perfect little brain-waker to start the day. I began by looking at that massive sum of 17 on the right side. Since the domino list only had a few high numbers like the 4-6 and the 3-6, I knew those big sixes had to go in that column. I placed a 6 in cell 2,3 and another 6 in cell 3,3, then grabbed the 5 from the 5-1 domino to fill the 1,3 spot. It felt so good to see that 17 click into place right away.

After that, the rest of the board was like putting together a very small map. I had the 1-1 domino left, and I placed it at 2,0 and 2,1 where those empty spaces were. The sum of 4 in the middle was easy to finish once I realized the 2-1 domino and the remaining half of the 3-6 domino were the only things left that would fit. It is funny how those big numbers really dictate where everything else has to go!

medium.heading: Stepping Up The Challenge
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today definitely stepped things up! I found myself scratching my head over the equals regions for a bit. There was one spot where three cells (1,3, 1,4, and 2,4) all had to be exactly the same value. I looked at my pile of dominoes and saw that I could use parts of the 4-3 and 6-3 dominoes to put 3s in those spots. Once I got those identical numbers lined up, the whole middle of the grid started looking much cleaner.

The trickiest part for me was the region at the bottom left that needed to be greater than 10. I saved my 6-0 and 6-3 dominoes specifically for that corner. By placing the 6 from the 6-3 domino at 1,0 and the 6 from the 6-0 domino at 2,0, I hit a sum of 12, which cleared the target easily. I ended the puzzle by using the double 1s to satisfy the sum of 2 at the very top. It was a nice little victory to have before my second cup of coffee!

hard.heading: A Real Monday Morning Head Scratcher
hard.body:
Wow, today's hard puzzle by Rodolfo Kurchan was a real journey! I actually had to start and stop a few times before I found my rhythm. The breakthrough for me was the column on the far left where cells 5,0, 6,0, and 7,0 all had to be equal. I ended up using the 1-1 domino and the 1 from the 1-3 domino to make them all 1s. This was a great anchor point that let me branch out into the surrounding sum regions that needed to hit totals of 4 and 5.

The middle of the grid was a bit of a jigsaw puzzle with all those small sums. I spent a lot of time toggling the 2-2 and 4-0 dominoes to see which one belonged in which sum region. I finally realized that the 5-4 and 1-5 dominoes were essential for hitting the greater than 5 and sum of 5 targets at the top. It felt like a giant chain reaction once those top dominoes were finally positioned correctly. If you get stuck on a grid this big, I definitely recommend focusing on the regions that require three identical numbers first!

explanation.tips: Always look for the highest sum regions first because they usually only have one or two possible combinations of dominoes. If you see an equals region, check your domino list for numbers that appear multiple times, like doubles or pairs of different dominoes with the same pip value. Don't be afraid to work from the corners inward, as the edges often have fewer ways to be filled.
explanation.learned: I learned today that equals regions are actually more helpful than sum regions because they act like a bridge that connects different parts of the board using the same value. I also noticed that high-value targets like the 17 in the easy puzzle are your best friends for narrowing down choices quickly.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You solve it by placing dominoes from the provided list onto the grid so that the numbers match the rules in each colored region, such as sums, equality, or greater-than targets.

faqs.question: What does the equals sign mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: The equals sign means every cell inside that specific colored region must have the exact same number of pips.

faqs.question: Can you reuse dominoes in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: No, each domino in the list for that day can only be used once to fill the grid.

faqs.question: What is the best way to start a hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: The best way to start is by looking for regions with very high or very low targets, or regions that require several cells to be equal, as these have the fewest possible solutions.

faqs.question: What does a target number with a greater than symbol mean?
faqs.answer: It means the total sum of all the pips in that colored region must be more than the target number shown.
